how-llms-work: Tokenization converts text into tokens—integer IDs the model understands. Tokens may be words, subwords, or characters depending on the tokenizer. Everything an LLM reads or writes is mediated by this segmentation, which affects cost, context limits, and awkward splits of rare words.
Like cutting a paragraph into LEGO bricks before a machine rebuilds meaning from brick IDs.
Tokenizers map text to token ID sequences and back.
Subword schemes balance vocabulary size and coverage.
Token counts drive context usage and pricing.
Weird splits can hurt reasoning on codes, names, or math.
Atomic text unit for the model
Algorithm mapping text to token IDs
Fragment smaller than a full word
A verbose prompt costs more even if word count looks modest.
What the model can name, and how much it can see

Vocabulary is the finite set of tokens a model knows IDs for. The context window is how many tokens of prompt, history, and generation the model can consider at once. If information falls outside the window, the model cannot directly use it unless you retrieve or summarize it back in.
Vocabulary is the dictionary of bricks; context window is the size of the table you can build on.
Finite vocab plus subword strategies cover open text.
Context window is a hard capacity constraint.
Long context helps but is not perfect memory.
Attention cost scales with context length.
Oldest turns get truncated or summarized.
Agents summarize old turns to stay inside context.
It must be truncated, summarized, or retrieved later
Longer context always means perfect recall.

how-llms-work: Meaning as coordinates in vector space

Embeddings are numeric vectors representing tokens, sentences, or documents so similar meanings land nearby geometrically. Models use embeddings internally; retrieval systems also embed queries and docs to find neighbors. Distances become a proxy for semantic relatedness.
A city map for meaning: doctor sits nearer nurse than screwdriver.
Embedding layer maps token IDs to vectors.
Cosine similarity is a common closeness measure.
Dimensionality and data shape the geometry.
Forums embed posts to find near-duplicate asks.
Tell the model token order matters
Self-attention alone does not inherently know order. Positional encodings (sinusoidal, learned, RoPE, ALiBi, and others) inject order so “dog bites man” differs from “man bites dog.”
Like page numbers in a shuffled manuscript—bricks need positions to rebuild the plot.
Attention mixes tokens; positions disambiguate order.
Modern LLMs often use rotary embeddings (RoPE).
Length generalization depends on the scheme.
Rotary position embedding used in many LLMs
Long-context behavior depends on the method.
Swapping two args changes meaning; positions preserve that.
Order is semantics in language and code.
A positional method used in many LLMs
Dog bites man vs man bites dog shows…
Each token gathers relevant context from others

Self-attention lets every token build a new representation by taking a weighted mix of other tokens information. Weights come from compatibility between queries and keys; values carry the content mixed in. This is how context disambiguates words like bank.
In a meeting, you glance more at people relevant to your current sentence—not equally at everyone forever.
Query, Key, Value projections create attention scores.
Causal masks prevent looking ahead in decoders.
Attention is powerful but quadratic in sequence length.
Each token makes Q, K, V.
Attention helps bind pronouns to the right noun.
Context selection is core to understanding.
Lets tokens gather info from other tokens
Looking at future tokens while decoding

Multi-head attention runs several attention operations in parallel, each potentially specializing in different relationship types, then concatenates results. More heads increase expressive capacity at a compute cost.
Multiple specialists reading the same paragraph: one tracks subjects, one tracks numbers, one tracks quotes.
Heads can specialize but are not guaranteed interpretable.
Different heads may track different alignment patterns.

After attention mixes information across tokens, a position-wise feed-forward network transforms each token vector independently. Intuitively, attention is communication; the FFN is private computation.
Group discussion (attention) then each person quietly rewrites their notes (FFN).
FFN applies the same MLP at each position.
Pairs with attention inside each block.
Holds substantial parameter count in LLMs.
Attention plus FFN unit with residuals/norms
Studies suggest FFNs play a large role in storing associations.
Attention routes; FFNs often compute and store.
Across users private emails by default
Attention mixes across tokens; FFN transforms each
Add the input back to ease deep training
Residual connections add a block input to its output so layers learn residual updates rather than whole transformations from scratch. This stabilizes deep stacks and improves gradient flow.
Editing with track changes: keep the original and add a delta instead of rewriting the whole essay each time.
Output is roughly input plus layer(input).
Used around attention and FFN sublayers.
Skip connection adding input to output
Attention or FFN unit inside a block
Residuals were key to training very deep nets.

Layer normalization rescales activations across features for each token so values stay well-behaved through deep stacks. Combined with residuals, it stabilizes training. Placement (pre-norm vs post-norm) varies by architecture.
Auto-adjusting microphone gain so each singer sits in a healthy volume range before the next effect pedal.
Normalize mean and variance across features.
Learned scale and bias restore flexibility.
Pre-norm is common in modern LLMs.
Norm choices affect convergence speed and stability.
Small engineering choices, large training impact.

Transformer families differ by attention layout. Encoder-only models bidirectional-encode inputs. Decoder-only models causally generate left-to-right. Encoder-decoder models encode a source then decode a target.
Encoder is reading comprehension; decoder is writing with only past drafts visible; encoder-decoder is read then write.
Choose by task: understand, generate, or transform.
Map an input sequence to an output sequence
Task appears: classify, chat, or translate.
Many NLP tasks cast as text-to-text with encoder-decoder models.
Layout follows the information flow you need.
Generate the next token using past tokens only
Autoregressive decoding produces tokens one by one, each conditioned on previously generated tokens and the prompt. That is why chat models stream words and why early mistakes can cascade.
Writing a sentence aloud without erasing: each new word must fit what you already said.
Predict token t given tokens before t.
UIs show partial answers as tokens arrive.
All tokens independently at once always
The core training and inference objective

Next-token prediction asks: given previous tokens, what is the probability distribution over the next token? Pretraining minimizes error on this task at scale; inference samples from it. Rich behaviors emerge without guaranteeing truth.
A fill-in-the-next-word game played billions of times until the player becomes an expert stylist of continuations.
Loss compares predicted distribution vs actual next token.
Capabilities emerge from objective plus data.
Calibration and factuality still need extra systems.
Prefix: The cat sat on the.
Model outputs scores for many tokens.
Productive continuation without understanding your whole company.
Fluent next tokens imply true facts.
Knobs that shape randomness of sampling

Decoding strategies reshape the next-token distribution. Temperature softens or sharpens probabilities. Top-k keeps only k highest tokens; top-p keeps the smallest set whose cumulative probability exceeds p. These knobs trade creativity versus stability.
Temperature is spice level; top-k and top-p cut off absurd ingredients.
Low temp is peaky; high temp is flatter.
Top-k and top-p truncate the tail.
Keep probability mass at least p
Optionally mask with top-k or top-p.
Marketing wants higher temperature; contracts want near-greedy decoding.
A dynamic nucleus of probability mass
The full prompt to sample to append cycle

The generation loop tokenizes the prompt, repeatedly samples a next token under the decoding policy, appends it, and stops on end-of-sequence, max length, or a stop string. Tool-using apps insert actions inside or around this loop.
A typewriter that guesses the next character, types it, then guesses again until it stops.
Tokens appear as the loop runs for perceived speed.
The prefix for the next prediction
Fluent guesses without grounded truth checks

Hallucinations happen because models optimize for plausible continuations, not verified world state. When context is missing or conflicting, the model still produces confident-sounding text. Decoding randomness, outdated data, and prompts that forbid uncertainty amplify the issue.
A skilled improv actor who never says I do not know unless trained to—and invents details to keep the scene going.
Objective is plausible tokens, not database lookup.
Gaps get filled with likely-sounding content.
Prompts can demand answers without uncertainty.
Mitigations include retrieval, tools, citations, refusals, and evals.
Tying answers to sources or tools
Prior patterns suggest a tidy answer.
Legal tools invented case law that looked real.
High-stakes domains need grounding and verification.
Optimizing plausible text without guaranteed grounding
Force an answer with no context
training-alignment: The raw fuel of model behavior

Datasets are collections of examples used to train or evaluate models. For LLMs this may be web text, books, code, instructions, or preference pairs. Data quality, licensing, diversity, and filters shape capabilities and harms more than most people expect.
You are what you eat—models absorb the statistics of their data diet.
Pretraining corpora are huge and noisy.
Fine-tune sets are smaller and task-focused.
Eval sets must not leak into training.
Governance covers consent, license, PII, and bias.
Training on repositories boosts coding help—and can memorize secrets if unfiltered.
Legal and ethical constraints bind training data

training-alignment.Web crawl dump: Scale plus noise plus legal risk.

training-alignment: Clean and shape raw data before training

Preprocessing turns messy raw sources into trainable examples: cleaning, filtering toxicity and PII, language detection, deduplication, formatting dialogues, and packing sequences. Bad preprocessing silently poisons quality.
Washing and measuring ingredients before cooking—the model only tastes what you prep.
Messages labeled system/user/assistant become supervised samples.
Choose a vocab that shapes learning
From a training view, tokenization is a compression and inductive-bias choice: vocabulary size and special tokens affect sequence lengths, rare word handling, multilingual fairness, and throughput.
Deciding whether your kitchen cuts veggies into cubes or ribbons—same ingredients, different cooking dynamics.
Special tokens mark roles and boundaries.
Frozen tokenizers couple to embedding matrices.
Tiny English-heavy vocab can over-fragment other languages.
A loss function measures how wrong predictions are. For LLMs, cross-entropy versus the true next token is standard. Training iteratively reduces loss—it does not directly maximize truth or safety.
A coach scorecard: mistakes add penalty points; practice aims to lower the score.
Loss quantifies error for gradient updates.
Low loss is a proxy, not a virtue metric.
Penalty for low probability on the true token
Evaluation measure that may differ from loss
Loss can look fine on frequent patterns while rare facts stay wrong.
Lower loss always means ethical behavior.
Nudge parameters downhill on the loss surface

Gradient descent updates parameters in the direction that locally decreases loss. The gradient indicates downhill; learning rate controls step size. Deep learning uses stochastic mini-batch estimates.
Hiking down a foggy mountain: feel the slope, take a step, repeat—avoid leaping into a ravine with a huge learning rate.
Compute gradient of loss versus parameters.
Bowl the optimizer may settle in
Smooth descending loss suggests healthy LR; explosions suggest trouble.
One batch of all Earth data always
Efficiently compute gradients through the net
Backpropagation applies the chain rule to compute how each parameter affected the loss, reusing intermediate calculations. Forward pass computes predictions; backward pass propagates error signals.
Tracing a cooking fail backward: salty soup, who added salt, which step, adjust that step next time.
Vanishing and exploding gradients challenged depth historically.
PyTorch and JAX compute grads via autograd graphs.
You design the graph; backprop fills gradients.
Automatic differentiation of the compute graph
Optimizers decide how to turn gradients into parameter updates. SGD, Momentum, Adam, and AdamW add adaptive step sizes and regularization behaviors that affect speed, stability, and final quality.
Not just walk downhill, but whether you use hiking poles or adapt stride to terrain.
SGD is simple and sometimes sharp.
Adam and AdamW adapt per-parameter rates.
Adaptive optimizer with decoupled weight decay
Optimizer and schedule tweaks prevent costly divergences.
Optimization is part of the research.
Adaptive steps and weight decay work well
Data is processed in batches. An epoch is one pass over the training set. Learning rate schedules change step size over time. For LLMs, tokens seen often matters more than epoch count.
Gym plan: sets are batches, full routines are epochs, and weekly weight is the LR schedule.
Batch size trades noise versus compute.
Token budgets dominate LLM training talk.
Plan for learning rate over time
Too-high early LR destabilizes; warmup ramps gently.
A group of examples per step

Pretraining teaches general patterns from massive data. Fine-tuning continues training on narrower data to specialize behavior. Most products adapt a pretrained base because pretraining is extremely expensive.
Learn general literacy first, then take a professional short course.
Parameter-efficient methods often beat full fine-tunes.
Losing old skills while learning new
Start from a general LLM; fine-tune on de-identified note styles.
Do not pretrain from scratch for every app.
New training can erode old skills
Train from scratch for FAQ bot

Supervised Fine-Tuning trains the model on high-quality prompt-response examples so it follows instructions in a desired style. It turns a base completion model into a more helpful assistant before preference optimization.
Script rehearsal: show ideal dialogues until the actor hits the right tone and structure.
SFT on approved templates yields on-brand support drafts.
Fine-tune small adapters instead of all weights
LoRA freezes most base weights and trains tiny low-rank adapter matrices, cutting memory and storage. QLoRA quantizes the base model while training adapters, enabling fine-tuning on smaller GPUs.
Instead of rewriting an entire textbook, stick removable sticky notes you can swap per subject.
QLoRA uses a quantized base plus adapters.
Swap adapters per task or tenant.
One base plus many per-customer adapters.
Align with human preferences via rewards

Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback fits a reward model on human preference comparisons, then optimizes the LLM policy to score higher while staying close to a reference model. It can improve helpfulness but is complex and can over-optimize quirks.
A comedy writer tries jokes, audience ranks them, coach trains for crowd-pleasers without wandering off-character.
Optimize policy with RL plus KL penalty.
Expensive and sensitive to preference data.
Chat models became more instruction-following after preference tuning eras.
Prevent drifting too far from reference
Preference tuning without a full RL loop

Direct Preference Optimization fine-tunes on preferred versus rejected responses using a classification-style objective that avoids a separate RL loop. It is often simpler operationally than classic RLHF.
Show good versus bad answers and teach prefer this over that, without a separate scoreboard coach in an RL loop.
No explicit reward-model RL loop required.
Still depends on preference data quality.
Teams use DPO to nudge refusals without heavy RL ops.

Memorize too hard versus learn too little
Underfitting means the model is too simple or under-trained. Overfitting means it memorizes training quirks and fails to generalize. Watch train versus validation metrics for gaps.
Underfit: studying only chapter titles. Overfit: memorizing answer keys, then freezing on a new question.
Train and val curves diagnose fit.
Regularization and more data fight overfit.
More capacity or training can fix underfit.
LLMs can memorize; privacy and eval design matter.
Add data, regularize, or stop earlier.

prompt-engineering: Who is speaking in the dialogue format

Chat models are trained on roles: system sets policy and persona, user provides requests, assistant responds. Clear role separation improves control. System messages are powerful but not magical security boundaries.
A play script: stage directions (system), audience request (user), actor lines (assistant).
Do not treat system prompts as perfect sandboxing.
System: be brief and cite policy; user asks refund question.
Stuff secrets only in system prompt
Teach by giving zero to a few examples

Zero-shot asks the model to perform a task with instructions only. One-shot and few-shot provide example input-output pairs in the prompt so the model mirrors the pattern. Examples are a lightweight way to specify format and style without fine-tuning.
Showing a worked example on the blackboard before asking students to do the next problem.
Too many demos can crowd the context window.
Show three labeled tickets, then ask for the fourth label.
Examples specify the label taxonomy quickly.

Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting asks the model to reason in intermediate steps before the final answer. For multi-step problems, visible reasoning often improves accuracy—though steps can also look convincing while being wrong.
Show your work on a math quiz: intermediate lines catch arithmetic slips.
Can be combined with self-consistency or tools.
Students prompt think step by step for unit conversions.
CoT mainly asks the model to…

Self-consistency samples several chain-of-thought trajectories (usually with temperature) and selects the most common final answer. Agreement across diverse paths often beats one greedy reasoning trace.
Ask three study partners to solve independently, then trust the answer they converge on.
Multiple samples reduce unlucky reasoning slips.
The answer is a random GIF
Hundred samples for a yes/no FAQ

Tree of Thoughts explores multiple partial reasoning branches, evaluates them, and expands promising ones—more search-like than a single linear chain. It can improve hard planning problems at higher complexity and cost.
A chess player considers several move trees, prunes weak lines, and deepens strong ones.
ToT-style search helps certain planning puzzles.
Search wrappers sit around the LLM.
Compared with linear CoT, ToT is usually…

ReAct prompting structures outputs as interleaved Thought, Action, and Observation. The model plans, calls a tool, reads the result, and continues. It is a prompting pattern that later becomes the backbone of many agents.
A lab notebook: hypothesize, run an experiment, record the observation, then decide the next step.
Act with a tool or API.
Reduces pure hallucination on lookup tasks.
Thought needs weather; action calls API; observation guides clothing advice.
Break a job into staged prompts

Prompt chaining splits a complex task into stages where each prompt’s output feeds the next: extract, transform, verify, format. Smaller steps are easier to control, test, and cache than one mega-prompt.
An assembly line: cut, assemble, paint, inspect—rather than one chaotic workshop moment.
Extract requirements, draft sections, compliance check, then polish.

Structured outputs ask the model to return JSON, tables, or schema-valid objects so software can parse results reliably. Schemas, constrained decoding, and validators turn prose generators into API-friendly components.
Fill a form with labeled fields instead of writing a free-form essay your parser cannot read.
Return vendor, date, total as JSON for accounting software.
type Invoice = { vendor: string; total: number }

Role prompting assigns a persona (tutor, reviewer, SRE) while constraints specify hard rules: length limits, banned topics, citation requirements, or tool-only claims. Constraints matter more than theatrical personas.
Costume plus safety rules: the costume sets tone; the rules keep the performance legal.
Conflicts between style and safety need priority order.
Add constraints: no final exam answers verbatim.
Tutor role with ban on full answer dumps.
Design what enters the window on purpose

Context engineering is the discipline of selecting, compressing, ordering, and refreshing what the model sees: instructions, tools, retrieved docs, memory, and user state. Prompts are only one ingredient; the whole window is the product.
Packing a backpack for a hike: bring the map and snacks that matter, leave the encyclopedias.
Order matters; put critical rules where models attend reliably.
Rules files, open tabs, and retrieved chunks are curated into context.
Engineering the window beats prompt poetry alone.
How prompts go wrong in practice

Prompts fail through ambiguity, conflicting instructions, missing constraints, format drift, jailbreak pressure, and overlong clutter. Treat prompts like code: test, version, and monitor regressions when models change.
Vague homework instructions that get five different interpretations from five students.
Model upgrades can invalidate prompt assumptions.
Old prompt fails on new model
“Make it pop” produced chaos until length, audience, and CTA were specified.
rag: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) fetches relevant documents at query time and conditions the model on that evidence. It reduces reliance on parametric memory for private or changing facts and makes citations possible.
An open-book exam: instead of memorizing every page, look up the chapter you need, then write the answer.
LLMs have stale or missing private knowledge.
Enables citations and updates without full retraining.
Still fails if retrieval misses or context is misused.
Employees ask about leave; answers come from the latest handbook chunks.
Update docs without retraining the LLM.

Chunking splits documents into passages sized for embedding and context budgets. Too large and retrieval is noisy; too small and meaning fragments. Overlap and structure-aware splits (headings, code functions) often help.
Indexing a textbook by coherent sections instead of one giant blob or single sentences with no context.
Choose chunk size for embedder and LLM.
Split by endpoint sections so retrieval returns whole endpoint explanations.
Encode queries and chunks into one space

Retrieval embeddings map queries and document chunks into a shared vector space so similar meanings neighbor each other. Embedding model choice, domain fit, and instruction formats strongly affect recall.
Library call numbers for meaning: related books shelved near each other so you can walk to the right aisle.
Did we fetch the needed evidence?
Semantic search finds issues describing the same crash with different words.
Store and search embeddings at scale

A vector database stores embeddings plus metadata and supports nearest-neighbor search at scale. It is the index behind most RAG stacks. Think retrieval engine, not a replacement for your system of record.
A specialized card catalog for coordinates of meaning, with filters for author and date.
Upsert vectors with IDs and metadata.
ANN algorithms trade exactness for speed.
Still need the original text store.
Insert or update a vector record
Teams store millions of chunk vectors with ACL metadata filters.
Vector DB replaces your source docs store.
It indexes; source of truth remains elsewhere.
Find nearest neighbors to a query vector
Similarity search ranks stored vectors by closeness to the query embedding using metrics like cosine similarity or inner product. Top-k results become candidate passages for the LLM.
Standing at a map pin and asking who is closest to me.
Similar past answers retrieved for new tickets.
Cosine similarity cares a lot about…

Hybrid search blends lexical matching (BM25/keywords) with vector similarity. Keywords catch exact IDs and rare terms; vectors catch paraphrases. Fusion methods merge ranked lists into a stronger candidate set.
Using both the index at the back of a book and a librarian who understands meaning.
Query has a SKU and a symptom.
Order IDs need keywords; fuzzy symptom descriptions need vectors.
Re-ranking takes a broader candidate set from cheap retrieval and scores each query-document pair with a stronger model. It improves precision before the LLM sees context, at extra compute cost.
A first pass grabs 50 library books quickly; an expert skims and keeps the best 5.
Score pairs with a cross-encoder or LLM judge.
Model scoring a query-doc pair together
Re-rankers prioritize truly on-point case passages.
The context budget is how many tokens you can afford for instructions, history, retrieved chunks, and the answer. RAG quality often hinges on what you include and exclude under that budget.
A fixed-size suitcase: folding and choosing beats bringing the whole closet.
Measure token costs of each section.
Smaller windows force aggressive chunk selection.

A retrieval pipeline chains ingest, chunk, embed, index, retrieve, (rerank), prompt assembly, generate, and cite. Production RAG is this pipeline plus evaluation and access control—not a single API call.
A newsroom workflow: archive stories, index them, research for a question, then write with sources.
Evals measure retrieval and answer quality.
Pipeline refreshes nightly as wiki pages change.
Builds grounded context for the LLM

Agentic RAG lets the model decide when and what to retrieve, possibly running multiple search steps, comparing sources, or asking clarifying questions. It is more flexible than one-shot retrieve-then-read, and more failure-prone without limits.
A researcher who searches, reads, realizes a gap, searches again, then writes—not a single Google query.
Agent pulls market notes then pricing pages before drafting.
RAG fails when chunking is bad, embeddings miss, filters exclude the truth, context is noisy, the model ignores evidence, or citations are fabricated. Evaluate retrieval and generation separately.
An open-book exam where you grab the wrong chapter, or read the right chapter and still misquote it.
Missed retrieval: answer has no chance.
Refusal to use evidence: ungrounded prose.

How up to date the store is

ai-agents: A model that acts toward goals with tools

An AI agent is a system that uses a model to pursue a goal by planning, calling tools, observing results, and updating state until it finishes or stops. It is more than a single reply; it is a loop with side effects.
An intern with a checklist and phone access: think, call someone, update the checklist, repeat.
External capability the agent can invoke
Agent searches flights, compares, then drafts an itinerary.
Acts in a loop with tools toward a goal
Reply once versus act over time

A chatbot mainly returns a next message. An agentic system can take multi-step actions, maintain state, and use tools across turns. Many products are hybrids: chat UI with optional agent modes for harder jobs.
Answering a question at a help desk versus actually filing the ticket, checking status, and emailing you.
Risk and cost rise with actions.
Pick the simplest mode that works.
Conversational interface mostly without side effects
User asks to book and email.
Balances answered in chat; transfers require agentic flows plus approvals.
Most agents iterate: plan what to do, act via a tool or message, observe the outcome, then replan. This loop turns a static model into an interactive problem solver—and can loop forever without caps.
Cooking while tasting: plan spice, act with a pinch, observe taste, adjust.
Plans column fixes, runs scripts, observes errors, replans.
What the agent remembers between steps

State is structured memory the agent updates: goals, scratchpads, tool results, file pointers, and status flags. Good state design makes agents debuggable; stuffing everything into chat text alone becomes fragile.
A pilot checklist and instrument panel—not only remembered conversation vibes.
Separate chat transcript from structured state.
Keep secrets out of prompts when possible.
State tracks which sources were read and remaining questions.
Decide the sequence before thrashing tools
Planning decomposes a goal into steps before or between actions. Plans can be implicit in thoughts or explicit checklists. Overplanning wastes tokens; underplanning causes tool thrash.
Writing grocery sections before wandering every aisle at random.
Share plan with users for trust.
Plan schema changes before running migrations.
Persist useful information beyond one prompt

Agent memory stores information across steps or sessions: conversation summaries, user preferences, retrieved facts, and episode logs. Memory systems must handle freshness, privacy, and relevance—or they become cluttered noise.
Sticky notes, a diary, and a filing cabinet—not expecting perfect photographic recall every second.
Remembers a student struggles with recursion and adapts examples.
Useful memory needs consent and controls.

Tool-calling lets a model emit structured function calls that your runtime executes. Schemas describe arguments; the app returns observations. This is how models browse, calculate, or update systems—under your permission model.
A voice assistant that can dial APIs the way you dial apps—only the ones you installed and allowed.
Never expose unconstrained shell by default.
Permissions make tools safe enough to ship.
Agents that think and act in text traces
ReAct agents operationalize the Thought-Action-Observation pattern as a runtime loop with tools. Traces make debugging easier, but verbose thoughts can leak private reasoning and cost tokens.
A detective notebook: hypothesize, check a clue, write what was found, hypothesize again.
Parse carefully; models drift from format.
Agents follow ReAct to query metrics then suggest mitigations.
Multi-agent systems assign roles to multiple agents—researcher, coder, critic—that communicate. Specialization can improve quality, but coordination overhead, cost, and failure modes grow quickly.
A small studio: writer, editor, and fact-checker instead of one exhausted generalist.
Measure if multi-agent beats a single strong agent.
One agent writes tests, another reviews security.
In the supervisor pattern, a central agent routes subtasks to worker agents, aggregates results, and decides next steps. It simplifies control flow compared with fully peer-to-peer swarms.
A shift manager assigning tickets to specialists and combining their results.
Supervisor sends billing questions to billing tools agent.
Everyone can call everyone with no limits
Guardrails are checks that constrain inputs, tools, and outputs: allowlists, policy classifiers, regex validators, rate limits, and human approvals. They acknowledge that prompts alone are soft.
Guardrails on a mountain road: the driver still steers, but barriers prevent falling off cliffs.
Deny when unsure on high risk
Outputs scrub account numbers before chat display.
Deny when unsure on high risk
A standard way to plug tools and context

Model Context Protocol (MCP) is a conceptual standard for exposing tools, resources, and prompts to models through a consistent interface. The idea is portable capabilities: connect an IDE, docs server, or database gateway without bespoke glue each time.

Human-in-the-loop (HITL) inserts people at critical steps: approve spends, edit drafts, confirm deletions. Autonomy handles draft work; humans own irreversible or regulated actions.
Autopilot can fly, but a pilot takes over for landing in a storm.
Auto-approve tiny refunds; humans approve large ones.
Save progress to recover and audit
Checkpointing snapshots agent state after steps so runs can resume, branch, or audit. It is essential for long jobs and for replaying failures without redoing expensive tool calls.
Video game save points before boss fights.

Checkpoint every keystroke to public S3

Agents fail via loops, tool misuse, prompt injection from tool outputs, goal misinterpretation, cost explosions, and silent partial completion. Design budgets, validators, and evaluations for agent traces—not only final answers.

Trusting malicious tool text as instructions.
Untrusted pages attempted to override system rules.

A box of LEGO adapters for LLM apps: useful accelerators, not a substitute for design.
Great for prototypes; mind lock-in and opacity.

LangGraph models agent workflows as graphs with nodes, edges, and explicit state—useful for durable, branching, human-in-the-loop agent systems beyond linear chains.
A flowchart you can execute: boxes are steps, arrows are decisions, and sticky notes are state.

Data framework for LLM retrieval apps
LlamaIndex focuses on connecting LLMs to data: indexes, query engines, and retrieval abstractions. Conceptually reach for it when your core problem is document QA and structured data access patterns.
A librarian toolkit specialized for getting the right pages into the model’s hands.
Index lecture PDFs for student questions.
CrewAI popularizes multi-agent “crews” with roles, tasks, and collaboration patterns. Conceptually it is an orchestration layer for role-based agent teams, with the usual multi-agent tradeoffs.
Assigning producer, writer, and editor roles on a small film set.
Researcher gathers sources; writer drafts; editor polishes.

AutoGen (and similar systems) structure multi-agent applications as conversations between agents—including user proxies and tool-using assistants. The conversation metaphor makes patterns easy to sketch and easy to overcomplicate.
A group chat where each participant has a job and can call tools when needed.
One agent writes code; another runs tests via tools.

Agent Development Kits (such as Google’s ADK conceptually) package patterns for building, evaluating, and deploying agents with cloud-native integrations. Think batteries-included tooling around orchestration, tools, and ops—not a new model architecture.
A robotics starter kit: motors, sensors, and manuals so you build a robot faster than inventing parts.
Kits standardize how teams ship internal agents.
Scaffolding and tools for building agents
One interface across many model APIs

LiteLLM provides a unified API layer to call many LLM vendors with similar request shapes. Conceptually it reduces glue code when you want provider failover, routing, or simpler swaps—while you still handle prompts and safety.
A universal remote that speaks many TV brands’ dialects.
Helpful for failover and cost routing.
Does not solve evaluation by itself.
Teams fail over when one vendor rate-limits.
Call every vendor for every token blindly
Choose tools by job, not hype

Pick frameworks by your bottleneck: raw SDK for control, LangChain for composable prototypes, LangGraph for durable agent graphs, LlamaIndex for data/RAG-centric apps, multi-agent kits for role workflows, LiteLLM for provider portability. The winning choice is the thinnest stack you can operate.
Choosing kitchen tools: a chef’s knife covers most jobs; buy a pasta machine only if you make pasta weekly.
Add orchestration when state gets hard.
RAG FAQ → LlamaIndex/light RAG; HITL agent → graph; multi-provider → LiteLLM.
deployment: Clients talk to your app, app talks to models

Serving an LLM app usually means your backend receives user requests, applies auth and policies, builds prompts/context, calls a model endpoint, streams tokens back, and logs traces. The model may be hosted by you or a cloud provider.
A restaurant: customers talk to waiters (your API), kitchen (model) cooks, food comes out in courses (streams).
Separate product logic from model vendor.
Design for timeouts and partial failures.
Web UI hits a FastAPI service that calls a hosted LLM with RAG.
Your app is the product boundary.
Your raw cloud keys in the browser
Python APIs that orchestrate LLM calls

FastAPI is a popular Python web framework for building async APIs—commonly used as the orchestration layer for LLM apps: routes, auth, validation, and streaming responses. Conceptually any solid API framework can play this role.
The waiter station: takes orders in a standard format and coordinates the kitchen.
Not the model itself—just the app layer.
Students expose /ask endpoints wrapping OpenAI-compatible APIs.
Package the app and its dependencies

Docker packages your application, runtime, and dependencies into images that run as containers. For LLM apps, containers make API services portable across laptops and clouds—while model weights may still live on volumes or remote APIs.
A shipping container for software: same box runs on different ships (machines).
“Works on my machine” fades when classmates run the same image.
Injected at runtime, not baked in
Bake API keys into the image

Kubernetes (K8s) schedules and manages containers across machines: deploy replicas, restart crashes, expose services, and scale. LLM apps may put API replicas on K8s while inference runs on GPU nodes or external APIs.
An air-traffic control system for containers—landing, scaling, and restarting workloads.
API autoscales during exam week traffic spikes.
You only have a static HTML file

Amazon Bedrock is a managed service to call foundation models via AWS APIs without self-hosting GPUs. Conceptually: provider-hosted inference with cloud IAM, networking, and billing integrated into AWS.
Ordering kitchen output from a hotel that already runs industrial kitchens—you bring recipes (prompts), they run stoves.
Still build your orchestration and RAG.
Teams adopt Bedrock to stay inside existing AWS controls.

Vertex AI is Google Cloud’s platform for ML and generative AI services—model APIs, tooling, and MLOps integrations. Conceptually similar tradeoff: managed capabilities inside a cloud ecosystem versus self-hosting.
A city workshop district with shared power tools—you build products using the district’s infrastructure.
Ties into GCP IAM and networking.
Use Vertex model APIs with BigQuery-stored logs.

Azure AI services provide managed model and AI capability APIs in Microsoft’s cloud, often attractive to enterprises already on Azure and Microsoft identity. Same mental model: managed inference plus your orchestration.
Building inside an office park that already has power, security badges, and utilities.
Enterprises host approved deployments on Azure.
Identity and compliance drive cloud choice.
You are invested in Microsoft cloud/identity
Use cloud identity with managed models
Streaming delivers tokens to clients as they are produced, improving perceived latency and enabling cancelation. Implement with server-sent events or websockets, and design UIs for partial answers.
Reading a story as it’s being typed instead of waiting for the whole novel PDF.
Streaming makes tutors feel responsive during long explanations.
Monitoring tracks request rates, latencies, error codes, token usage, and tool failures. Without it, LLM apps fail quietly and bills surprise you. Start with golden signals plus token economics.
A car dashboard: speed, fuel, warning lights—not driving blind.
Latency alerts reveal retrieval bottlenecks under load.
production-ai: Measure quality with tests, not vibes

Evaluation scores whether an AI system meets task requirements: automated metrics, LLM-as-judge carefully used, human review, and regression sets. Production teams treat evals like unit tests for behavior.
Exam questions for your product—run them before every release.
Separate retrieval vs generation scores for RAG.
Weekly eval suite blocks deploys that hurt math accuracy.

Observability captures traces, logs, and artifacts for each request: prompts, retrieved chunks, tool calls, latencies, and outputs (with privacy controls). It turns “the model was weird” into a debuggable timeline.
Flight data recorders for AI requests.
Why did it cite the wrong doc?
Trace shows reranker order flipped after a deploy.

LLM apps add threats: prompt injection, data exfiltration via tools, training data leakage, insecure key handling, and sensitive logs. Apply least privilege, isolation, redaction, and adversarial testing.
A building with doors, badges, cameras, and rules for contractors—not only a polite receptionist.
Never trust retrieved/web content as instructions.
Untrusted pages tried to exfiltrate secrets via tool calls.
Put keys in the mobile app

Mitigate hallucinations with grounding (RAG/tools), abstention (“I don’t know”), citation requirements, lower-stakes drafting roles, constrained decoding, and human review for high risk. No single trick eliminates them.
Journalism standards: require sources, allow “unknown,” and fact-check before publish.
Bot refuses diagnosis and cites approved leaflets only.
Hallucinations can be fully solved by one prompt sentence.
Answer only with citations or abstain
Production guardrails enforce policies at runtime: topic blocks, PII filters, tool allowlists, rate limits, and output validators. Layer them: before model, around tools, after generation.
Airport security lanes plus cockpit locks—multiple checkpoints.
PII filters block national IDs in outputs.

LLM cost is driven by tokens, model choice, retries, and tool calls. Optimize with caching, smaller models for easy tasks, tighter prompts, retrieval over long pastes, and routing hard cases to bigger models.
Household budgeting: stop leaving every light on; use the big oven only when needed.
FAQ intents use a small model; complex cases escalate.
All cases to the largest always
Make it fast enough under load

Latency comes from retrieval, model time-to-first-token, tool calls, and network hops. Scale with concurrency limits, caches, async jobs, streaming, and horizontal replicas—while watching queueing delays.
Grocery checkout: open more lanes at peak, and let people see items scanned live (streaming).
Caching syllabus chunks keeps RAG snappy.
Reliable AI systems define timeouts, retries with idempotency, fallbacks (smaller model, cached answer, human), and clear degraded modes. Models will error; products should not hard-crash.
City power grids with backup generators and polite “service degraded” banners.
If LLM down, show FAQ search fallback.

Before calling an AI feature “done,” check: threat model, eval suite, tracing, budgets, guardrails, fallbacks, privacy review, and on-call ownership. This checklist turns Generative AI from a demo into an engineered product.
Preflight checklist before takeoff—not optional theater.
Student teams use the checklist before showing faculty advisors.
